recent.narrative: A strong spring storm tracked across the region, producing areas of heavy snow across northeastern Wyoming. The heaviest snow fell across southern portions of Campbell County and Weston County, where six to 12 inches were reported in many areas. Amounts generally tapered off to the north across northeastern Wyoming. Gusty winds produced some blowing and drifting snow and reduced visibility at times.

A strong winter storm impacted the area, bringing significant snowfall, gusty winds, and a surge of Arctic air. A series of upper-level disturbances associated with the system overrode the Arctic air at the surface and produced snowfall for an extended period. The Arctic cold front dropped temperatures to near or below zero for an extended period. Snowfall amounts were in the six to 12 inch range across a good portion of northeastern Wyoming, with amounts tailing off some across far northeastern Wyoming. Minor blowing and drifting of snow occurred with breezy conditions. Wind chill values dropped to 20 below to 35 below zero during the event.

Snowfall amounts were mostly in the two to six inch range across the area, with locally higher amounts across the Bear Lodge Mountains and Wyoming Black Hills.

An Arctic cold front brought some snow, along with extremely low temperatures, strong winds, and bitter cold wind chills. Light amounts of new snow, along with considerable, blowable snowpack from the previous week's blizzard, combined with the strong winds to produce a period of blizzard or near blizzard conditions across the northeastern Crook County plains. Gusts over 40 mph developed during the daytime hours. Highway 212 was closed across the area during much of the day.

An Arctic airmass settled over the region, bringing bitter cold temperatures and gusty winds that produced wind chills of 30 below to 50 below zero at times from late day on the 20th through the 23rd.

A powerful winter storm moved slowly across the central and northern Plains into the Upper Midwest; bringing heavy snow, gusty winds, and near blizzard conditions at times in some areas over a multi-day period. Snowfall was heaviest over the Bear Lodge Mountains and far northeastern Wyoming, where one to two feet of snow was reported in most areas. Amounts tapered off toward southern and eastern portions of the Weston County plains, where only a few inches fell.  Gusty winds developed, especially on the 15th, causing considerable blowing and drifting snow. Travel became difficult at times in some areas, especially from Interstate 90 northward. Interstate 90 was closed several times for extended periods due to heavy snow in the northern Black Hills and blowing snow.

An upper-level system moved across the northern Rockies and northern Plains, bringing snowfall to mostly far northeast Wyoming. Snowfall amounts were highest across northern Campbell County and the Bear Lodge Mountains, where amounts up to 9 inches were reported.

An arctic cold front passed through the region, bringing very cold temperatures from the 18th to the morning of the 21st. The coldest temperatures and lowest wind chills were during the overnight and morning hours of the 20th. Temperatures dropped to 10 below to 30 below zero in many areas, with northerly winds of 15 to over 25 mph producing wind chill values as low as 30 below to around 50 below zero.

An upper-level trough and cold front swept through the region, bringing some snowfall and gusty winds to much of northeast Wyoming. A period of heavy upslope snowfall occurred during the daytime and evening hours on the 11th across the higher elevations of the Wyoming Black Hills and the Bear Lodge Mountains. Snowfall totals of 5 to 9 inches were reported across these areas, with 1 to 4 inches elsewhere across far northeast Wyoming. Gusty winds up to 40 mph produced some blowing snow and greatly reduced visibility at times. The snow and gusty winds caused travel impacts across the area.

A storm system brought widespread beneficial precipitation to most of northeast Wyoming. Temperatures became cold enough for rain to change over to snow fairly quickly during the daytime of the 29th, then persisted into the morning hours of the 30th. The heaviest snow fell during the afternoon and evening hours. Snowfall amounts were heaviest across portions of southern Campbell County and the Bear Lodge Mountains. The highest amounts were reported in the Wright and Sundance areas, 7 to 14 inches, with amounts to around 6 inches elsewhere across southern Campbell County, the Gillette and Moorcroft areas, and Crook and western Weston counties. Travel was most impacted across southern Campbell County and portions of Interstate 90.

A strong upper-level system moved slowly across the region, bringing beneficial precipitation to much of northeast Wyoming. Rain turned fairly quickly over to snow across the area during the late day and evening hours of the 6th. Snowfall was heaviest over much of Campbell County and the Bear Lodge Mountains, where 6 inches to around a foot of accumulation was reported. Gusty winds to around 50 mph produced some blowing snow during the morning hours of the 7th.

The Red Canyon fire started on the northern foothills of the Bridger Mountains in Hot Springs County on the afternoon of August 13th due to a lightning strike. The fire had grown to 3,000 acres by August 14th. A combination of hot and dry conditions as well as gusty wind caused the fire to exhibit extreme fire behavior and spread rapidly, especially on August 16th when several evacuations were ordered to the southeast of Thermopolis and fire spread from Hot Springs county into northern Fremont County. The fire had grown to over 100,000 acres by August 20th as the hot and dry conditions continued. Containment increased starting on August 22nd as cooler weather and higher humidity moved in. The fire was 80 percent contained by August 27th, and all evacuations and road closures were lifted. All in all, time Red Canyon fire burned nearly 125,000 acres.

Snowfall totals of 5 to 9 inches were common across the area, with localized amounts to around 12 inches. Amounts of 3 to 5 inches were noted in the Newcastle area.

Snowfall totals of 5 to 9 inches were reported across these areas, with 1 to 4 inches elsewhere across far northeast Wyoming. Gusty winds up to 40 mph produced some blowing snow and greatly reduced visibility at times. The snow and gusty winds caused travel impacts across the area.

A passing cold front and upper-level shortwave brought gusty northwest winds and colder air to the area. The gusty winds and moisture in place helped to produce a prolonged period of heavy upslope snowfall during the morning and afternoon hours across parts of the Wyoming Black Hills and Bear Lodge Mountains. Amounts of 5 to 12 inches were common across the higher Wyoming Black Hills, especially the Four Corners area to O'Neill Pass. Amounts of 2 to 6 inches fell over the rest of the Wyoming Black Hills, Bear Lodge Mountains and parts of northeast Crook County. The heavy snow impacted travel across a good part of the area during the daytime and evening hours.
